title: Foundation-to-algebra and early function relationships
status: AI-assisted preliminary desk review; educator confirmation pending
method_note: Classifications are draft curriculum-design judgements based on the stated concept outcomes and edge roles. They are not independent expert sign-off or empirical validation. The proposed tests are future checks, not completed experiments.

EDGE-029: Signed-rational arithmetic helps with later examples but is not needed to introduce the roles of variable, unknown, and parameter. Use whole-number contexts first; provide FND-015 as a repair path where calculations—not letter roles—block learning.
Teach the letter-role objective with whole-number contexts, then test a separate signed-rational transfer item. If only the second fails, do not treat FND-015 as a gate for ALG-001.
EDGE-030: Minimum symbol/statement literacy supports reading letters and translating between verbal and symbolic forms. For accessible self-study, teach this minimum within an ALG-001 bridge instead of denying entry.
Diagnostic: interpret x + 2 and translate 'a number plus 2'; provide a short notation bridge and retest variable/unknown/parameter distinctions.
EDGE-031: The meanings of variables and parameters are needed to interpret symbolic expressions and reason about equivalence; the two concepts may be scaffolded in adjacent lessons.
Ask learners to identify the role of a letter and explain why 2x + 3 and 3 + 2x are equivalent; record whether an ALG-001 refresh is enough.
EDGE-032: Numerical operation meanings and basic properties underpin interpretation and simplification of symbolic expressions. This requires operational meaning, not mastery of every arithmetic strand.
Move from 3 + 2 and 3 × 2 to 3x + 2x and equivalent forms; distinguish operation-meaning errors from notation errors.
EDGE-033: Exponent notation appears in some expressions, but initial expression meaning/equivalence can be learned without exponent laws. Introduce FND-014 just in time when powers enter.
Check the ALG-002 outcomes using expressions without exponents; verify that power laws are not secretly assumed before introducing them explicitly.
EDGE-034: Equations and inequalities relate expressions and constrain possible values, so expression interpretation and equivalence are foundational to the current mapped outcome.
Ask learners to interpret x + 2 = 5 and x + 2 < 5, distinguish expression from statement, and test candidate values.
EDGE-035: A signed number line is important for representing solution sets with negative values, but the meaning of an equation or inequality as a statement can be taught earlier. This cluster combines both tasks.
Assess separately: identify an equation/inequality as a constraint, then graph a solution set spanning negative and positive values. FND-006 is more essential for the latter.
EDGE-036: Solving equations depends on understanding them as constraints and preserving the solution set under valid transformations.
Have learners solve and verify a linear equation, then explain why a valid operation performed on both sides preserves equality.
EDGE-037: Full linear equation/inequality fluency with standard rational coefficients uses signed and rational arithmetic. Integer-only starter examples may precede it, but the complete ALG-004 outcome needs this capability or targeted repair.
Use equations with negative/fractional coefficients and sign-sensitive inequalities. Diagnose arithmetic errors separately and provide an FND-015 repair where needed.
EDGE-038: Rearranging literal formulas extends isolating an unknown through reversible equation transformations, the central capability developed in linear equation solving.
Rearrange a familiar formula for a different variable, substitute back, and check nonzero-denominator restrictions.
EDGE-039: Formula rearrangement requires learners to interpret and maintain equivalent symbolic expressions even when the target variable changes.
Give an equivalent-expression task before rearranging a literal formula; check whether the transformation reasoning transfers.
EDGE-040: Unit conversion and dimensional sense are not prerequisites for symbolic rearrangement itself; they are important for interpreting unit-bearing formulas and scientific applications.
Compare a pure-symbol rearrangement with a unit-bearing application; assess algebraic success separately from interpreting and checking units.
EDGE-041: The coordinate-plane outcome includes signed coordinates and points in all quadrants. Understanding signed values relative to zero is a direct conceptual support and can be bridged locally.
Ask learners to order signed values on a number line, then plot ordered pairs in all four quadrants; identify sign and axis errors.
EDGE-042: Basic notation helps with ordered pairs and coordinate labels, but these conventions are teachable inside the coordinate lesson. Do not make the entire FND-001 cluster a rigid gate.
Give a brief ordered-pair/axis primer and test plotting; compare error types before and after the local explanation.
EDGE-043: Graph literacy explicitly requires plotting/interpreting coordinates and relating graphs to tables, equations, and contexts; coordinate-plane fluency is a direct dependency.
Before graph-construction tasks, plot table values with labelled axes and scales; assess coordinate plotting separately from trend interpretation.
EDGE-044: Proportional relationships offer useful graphs through the origin, but graph literacy must cover non-proportional, nonlinear, and empirical graphs too.
Test graph interpretation on non-proportional lines, nonlinear curves, and empirical/categorical data as well as percentage examples.
EDGE-045: The current slope/rate outcome includes graph interpretation and proportional-versus-affine comparison; graph literacy supports axis/scale reading and representation changes.
Infer rate from a graph with nontrivial axis scales, confirm from a table, and separate graph-reading errors from rate-reasoning errors.
EDGE-046: Slope/rate of change is change-per-change; ratios and unit rates supply the conceptual basis for interpreting slope rather than memorizing rise-over-run.
Transfer from a unit-rate context and double number line to a table and graph; explain the ratio and its units.
EDGE-047: Unit/dimensional sense improves interpretation of slope and intercept units, but an initial slope concept can be taught on a unitless graph. The full measurement cluster is broader than the minimum prerequisite.
Assess calculation first and unit interpretation second; teach only the missing unit subskill locally when needed.
EDGE-048: A function can first be introduced through mappings, input-output tables, and uniqueness, without symbolic expressions. Expression skill is needed for formula representations.
Teach a mapping/table example before a formula; assess function recognition separately from interpretation of symbolic rules.
EDGE-049: Coordinates are needed for graphical representations of functions, not for the input-output/mapping definition itself. Multiple representations should provide more than one entry route.
Assess function recognition from mappings and tables before graph tasks; keep graph interpretation as a dependent sub-outcome.
EDGE-050: The mapped linear-function outcome uses slope/rate and the proportional-versus-affine distinction established in ALG-008.
From a table with constant first differences, build a linear rule, identify slope/intercept, and distinguish a line through the origin from one with nonzero intercept.
EDGE-051: In this curriculum, a general function concept supplies input-output, domain, and range language needed to position linear functions as one function family. Motivation with a linear example can still come first.
Compare linear and non-linear functions and a relation that fails uniqueness; check whether learners can explain the special case and its domain.
EDGE-052: Interpreting a linear function as an equation requires minimum fluency with equality as a relation and symbolic statements. Teach that minimum within the linear-function lesson if necessary.
Ask learners to read y = 2x + 3 as a relationship, explain what equality asserts, and interpret slope/intercept; note if a short bridge suffices.
EDGE-053: Substitution and elimination extend equation-solving transformations and depend on preserving equality while isolating or eliminating variables.
Have learners solve/check a one-variable linear equation before a system; code errors as equation-solving, sign, or system-model issues.
EDGE-054: The mapped systems outcome explicitly includes graphical solutions, which require coordinate plotting and reading intersection points. Algebraic methods may be introduced separately.
Solve a two-line system graphically and algebraically, then compare the intersection with the ordered-pair solution.
EDGE-055: Linear-function representations supply the line equations and intersection meaning used in graphical systems. This is core to the full multi-representation outcome, though substitution/elimination can be taught separately.
Plot two linear functions, identify their intersection, and substitute the ordered pair into both equations; assess algebra and graph-reading separately.
